title: Advanced Materials and Structural Analysis
data_note: Materials data from peer-reviewed literature and official sources. QCD and electromagnetic couplings are scale-dependent parameters in different theories and must not be interpreted as a ratio of chemical-bond or macroscopic tensile strengths.

source.name: Takakura, A. et al. Strength of carbon nanotubes depends on their chemical structures. Nature Communications 10, 3040 (2019) — cites the 100–200 GPa theoretical range

statistics.context: Range depends on chirality, diameter, and defect density of individual nanotubes.
statistics.verification_note: Theoretical limit; individual tube measurements approach this range

source.name: Bai, Y. et al. Nature Nanotechnology 13, 589 (2018)

statistics.context: Achieved in centimetre-long CNT bundles (wall-area basis; 43 GPa engineering). Highest reported for multi-tube bundles; individual MWCNT shells have reached ~100 GPa (Peng et al. 2008).

source.name: Takakura, A. et al. Strength of carbon nanotubes depends on their chemical structures. Nature Communications 10, 3040 (2019)

statistics.context: Among the stiffest known materials. The ideal-strength estimate of order E/10 gives ~100 GPa; this is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a strict upper bound.
statistics.verification_note: Widely reproduced across multiple independent measurements

source.name: Derived: 63 GPa (Yu et al., Science 287, 637, 2000) ÷ ~1,300 kg/m³; convention-dependent

statistics.context: Of order 10^4 kN·m/kg and convention-dependent: ~48,000 kN·m/kg for 63 GPa at a bulk density of ~1,300 kg/m³, or ~36,000 kN·m/kg for 80 GPa on a wall cross-section of graphitic density (~2,200 kg/m³); roughly 200–300× high-carbon steel (~154 kN·m/kg).
statistics.verification_note: Calculated from a measured tensile strength and an assumed density; the result depends on the strength cross-section and density convention.

statistics.context: Measured by AFM nanoindentation of suspended monolayer graphene membranes.
Stiffest known 2D material. Consistent with CNT measurements (same sp² carbon bonding).

statistics.metric: Ideal (theoretical) strength of a defect-free crystal (order-of-magnitude estimate)

source.name: Orowan, E. Fracture and strength of solids. Rep. Prog. Phys. 12, 185 (1949) — ideal cohesive strength ~E/10; cf. Frenkel, Z. Phys. 37, 572 (1926) for ideal shear strength ~G/2π

statistics.context: An order-of-magnitude estimate set by interatomic bonding, not a strict upper bound. For sp² carbon (E ~ 1 TPa) it gives ~100 GPa, comparable to the measured intrinsic strength of defect-free graphene (~130 GPa ≈ E/8).
statistics.verification_note: Classical order-of-magnitude estimate; graphene's measured ~E/8 shows that E/10 is not a strict limit. The previous source DOI (10.1007/BF01349680) resolved to an unrelated 1921 paper.

source.name: Bai, Y. et al. Nature Nanotechnology 13, 589-595 (2018) — single-bundle vs. macroscale fiber comparison

statistics.context: Gap between centimetre-long bundles (~80 GPa) and macroscale fibres (~few GPa) due to defects, weak inter-tube shear, processing.
statistics.verification_note: Widely reported in materials science literature

statistics.metric: Measured strength of structure-defined individual SWCNTs

source.name: Takakura, A. et al. Strength of carbon nanotubes depends on their chemical structures. Nature Communications 10, 3040 (2019)

statistics.context: Strength depends primarily on chiral structure; defects concentrate stress. Measured values fall well below the 100–200 GPa ideal predictions.
statistics.verification_note: Checked against Takakura et al. (2019), who measured 25–66 GPa for 16 structure-defined SWCNTs. The previously listed 'up to 85%' defect-induced reduction does not appear in that paper and was removed.

statistics.metric: Strong nuclear force coupling constant at nuclear scale
statistics.context: The QCD coupling runs with renormalization scale and becomes non-perturbative near confinement. A rough order-unity value at hadronic scales cannot be divided by the electromagnetic fine-structure constant to infer bond or material strength.
statistics.verification_note: PDG supports the running QCD coupling. The entry is a theory parameter, not a mechanical-property measurement.

statistics.context: The fine-structure constant characterizes electromagnetic interaction strength. Its ratio to a QCD coupling at another scale is not a ratio of bond energies or tensile strengths. Nuclear binding is confined to femtometre scales and does not imply a macroscopic material 100 times stronger than chemical solids.
statistics.verification_note: The constant is precisely measured; the previous 100x strong-force material inference was unsupported and has been removed.
